claim: Hox genes are essential regulators of embryonic development.
source: Hox genes are essential regulators of embryonic development.
evidence: This is a well-established fact in developmental biology, supported by extensive research cited throughout the manuscript.

claim: Transcriptional activation of Hox genes follows their genomic topology.
source: Their step-wise transcriptional activation follows their genomic topology and the various states of activation are subsequently memorized into domains of progressively overlapping gene products.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is a fundamental observation of the study.

claim: Initially, Hox clusters are organized as single chromatin compartments containing all genes and bivalent chromatin marks.
source: Initially, Hox clusters are organized as single chromatin compartments containing all genes and bivalent chromatin marks.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract and supported by 4C-seq and ChIP-seq data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Transcriptional activation is associated with a dynamic bi-modal 3D organization, whereby the genes switch autonomously from an inactive to an active compartment.
source: Transcriptional activation is associated with a dynamic bi-modal 3D organization, whereby the genes switch autonomously from an inactive to an active compartment.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by 4C-seq data comparing different developmental stages shown in Figures 2-4.

claim: Local 3D dynamics occur within a framework of constitutive interactions within the surrounding Topological Associated Domains.
source: These local 3D dynamics occur within a framework of constitutive interactions within the surrounding Topological Associated Domains, indicating that this regulation process is mostly cluster intrinsic.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by long-range interaction analysis presented in Figure 5.

claim: The step-wise progression in time is fixed at various body levels and can account for chromatin architectures at later stages for different anterior to posterior levels.
source: The step-wise progression in time is fixed at various body levels and thus can account for the chromatin architectures previously described at a later stage for different anterior to posterior levels.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by comparison of temporal and spatial samples in Figures 3-4.

claim: Mouse and human Hox genes are organized in four genomic clusters (HoxA to HoxD).
source: Mouse and human Hox genes are organized in four genomic clusters (HoxA to HoxD), where the relative position of the genes strongly impacts upon their patterns of expression.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations.

claim: The relative position of Hox genes strongly impacts upon their patterns of expression.
source: Mouse and human Hox genes are organized in four genomic clusters (HoxA to HoxD), where the relative position of the genes strongly impacts upon their patterns of expression.
evidence: This is a fundamental principle of Hox gene regulation, supported by extensive literature.

claim: The structure-function relationship of Hox genes was initially described in Drosophila.
source: This structure-function relationship was initially described in Drosophila (Lewis, 1978) and further extended to vertebrates (Gaunt et al., 1988; Duboule and Dolle, 1989; Graham et al., 1989), where an additional correspondence exists between gene position and the timing of transcriptional activation ('temporal colinearity', Izpisua-Belmonte et al., 1991; Deschamps and van Nes, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by the citation to Lewis, 1978.

claim: In vertebrates, there is a correspondence between Hox gene position and the timing of transcriptional activation, termed 'temporal colinearity'.
source: This structure-function relationship was initially described in Drosophila (Lewis, 1978) and further extended to vertebrates (Gaunt et al., 1988; Duboule and Dolle, 1989; Graham et al., 1989), where an additional correspondence exists between gene position and the timing of transcriptional activation ('temporal colinearity', Izpisua-Belmonte et al., 1991; Deschamps and van Nes, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations including Izpisua-Belmonte et al., 1991 and Deschamps and van Nes, 2005.

claim: In murine embryos, transcription of Hox genes is first detected at around embryonic day 7 (E7) at the most posterior aspect of the primitive streak region.
source: In murine embryos, transcription of Hox genes can be divided in several phases and is first detected at around embryonic day 7 (E7) at the most posterior aspect of the primitive streak region (Deschamps and Wijgerde, 1993; Forlani et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Deschamps and Wijgerde, 1993 and Forlani et al., 2003.

claim: Hox genes are sequentially activated following their chromosomal order over time.
source: Over time, Hox genes are sequentially activated following their chromosomal order and transcripts encoded by the last Hox group 13 genes can be detected at around E9, that is two days after the onset of activation (Deschamps et al., 1999; Kmita and Duboule, 2003; Deschamps and van Nes, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations and is a fundamental observation of temporal colinearity.

claim: Transcripts encoded by Hox group 13 genes can be detected at around E9, two days after the onset of activation.
source: Over time, Hox genes are sequentially activated following their chromosomal order and transcripts encoded by the last Hox group 13 genes can be detected at around E9, that is two days after the onset of activation (Deschamps et al., 1999; Kmita and Duboule, 2003; Deschamps and van Nes, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Deschamps et al., 1999; Kmita and Duboule, 2003; Deschamps and van Nes, 2005.

claim: The transcriptional progression of Hox genes (the 'Hox clock') extends over several days.
source: This transcriptional progression (the 'Hox clock', Duboule, 1994) thus extends over several days.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citation to Duboule, 1994.

claim: In the pre-somitic mesoderm (PSM), sequential Hox activation needs to be coordinated with the time-sequenced production of body segments (the 'segmentation clock').
source: In the pre-somitic mesoderm (PSM), this sequential activation needs to be coordinated with the time-sequenced production of body segments (the 'segmentation clock', Pourquie, 2003), such that newly produced somites acquire distinct genetic identifiers (Dubrulle et al., 2001; Zakany et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pourquie, 2003; Dubrulle et al., 2001; Zakany et al., 2001.

claim: Newly produced somites acquire distinct genetic identifiers through coordination of Hox and segmentation clocks.
source: In the pre-somitic mesoderm (PSM), this sequential activation needs to be coordinated with the time-sequenced production of body segments (the 'segmentation clock', Pourquie, 2003), such that newly produced somites acquire distinct genetic identifiers (Dubrulle et al., 2001; Zakany et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dubrulle et al., 2001 and Zakany et al., 2001.

claim: Various states of Hox gene activity are fine-tuned and memorized, leading to domains along the rostral to caudal axis with partially overlapping sets of HOX products ('spatial colinearity').
source: Next, the various states of Hox gene activity are fine-tuned and memorized, ultimately leading to domains along the rostral to caudal axis where partially overlapping sets of HOX products can be observed ('spatial colinearity').
evidence: This is a description of spatial colinearity, a well-established concept in Hox gene biology.

claim: Genes located at 3′ positions (e.g., groups 3, 4) are transcribed almost along the entire embryonic axis.
source: As a result, genes located at 3′positions (e.g., groups 3, 4) are transcribed almost along the entire embryonic axis, including the lateral plate mesoderm, paraxial mesoderm and neural tube, whereas the 5′-located group 10 or 11 are active in the posterior trunk and group 13 in the tip of the tail bud only (Deschamps et al., 1999; Kmita and Duboule, 2003; Deschamps and van Nes, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Deschamps et al., 1999; Kmita and Duboule, 2003; Deschamps and van Nes, 2005.

claim: 5′-located Hox group 10 or 11 genes are active in the posterior trunk.
source: As a result, genes located at 3′positions (e.g., groups 3, 4) are transcribed almost along the entire embryonic axis, including the lateral plate mesoderm, paraxial mesoderm and neural tube, whereas the 5′-located group 10 or 11 are active in the posterior trunk and group 13 in the tip of the tail bud only (Deschamps et al., 1999; Kmita and Duboule, 2003; Deschamps and van Nes, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Deschamps et al., 1999; Kmita and Duboule, 2003; Deschamps and van Nes, 2005.

claim: Hox group 13 genes are active in the tip of the tail bud only.
source: As a result, genes located at 3′positions (e.g., groups 3, 4) are transcribed almost along the entire embryonic axis, including the lateral plate mesoderm, paraxial mesoderm and neural tube, whereas the 5′-located group 10 or 11 are active in the posterior trunk and group 13 in the tip of the tail bud only (Deschamps et al., 1999; Kmita and Duboule, 2003; Deschamps and van Nes, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Deschamps et al., 1999; Kmita and Duboule, 2003; Deschamps and van Nes, 2005.

claim: Temporal and spatial colinear processes likely reflect one and the same organizational principle.
source: While both temporal and spatial colinear processes likely reflect one and the same organizational principle, they are nevertheless implemented with distinctive features.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on the relationship between temporal and spatial colinearity.

claim: Spatial colinearity could be recapitulated by several single-gene transgenes in some instances.
source: Spatial colinearity could be recapitulated by several single-gene transgenes (e.g., [Puschel et al., 1991; Whiting et al., 1991]), yet not in all instances (Tschopp et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Puschel et al., 1991; Whiting et al., 1991; and Tschopp et al., 2012.

claim: At a late stage, sustained transcription of Hox genes at the correct body level primarily relies upon local regulatory elements.
source: Indeed, a systematic analysis of modified HoxD clusters in vivo revealed that, at a late stage, the sustained transcription of these genes at the correct body level primarily relies upon local regulatory elements (Tschopp et al., 2009), which are present in transgenic constructs.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tschopp et al., 2009.

claim: The precise timing of Hoxd gene activation depends on the integrity of the full cluster.
source: In contrast, the precise timing of Hoxd gene activation depends on the integrity of the full cluster, a genomic situation observed thus far in all animals developing following a temporal rostral to caudal progressive strategy during their early development (Duboule, 1994).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Duboule, 1994.

claim: The genomic clustering of Hox genes is an essential feature for temporal colinearity to properly process.
source: The genomic clustering of Hox genes is thus considered as an essential feature for temporal colinearity to properly process, whereas it may not be as important for the correct distribution of HOX products along the AP-axis, at least in the late phase of spatial colinearity (Duboule, 2007; Tschopp et al., 2009; Noordermeer and Duboule, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Duboule, 2007; Tschopp et al., 2009; Noordermeer and Duboule, 2013.

claim: In embryonic stem (ES) cells, Hox clusters are decorated by both repressive (H3K27me3) and activating (H3K4me3) marks.
source: In embryonic stem (ES) cells, that is cells that reflect best the state of Hox genes before their activation, Hox clusters are decorated by both repressive (H3K27me3) and activating (H3K4me3) marks (Bernstein et al., 2006; Schuettengruber et al., 2007; Soshnikova and Duboule, 2009; Noordermeer and Duboule, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bernstein et al., 2006; Schuettengruber et al., 2007; Soshnikova and Duboule, 2009; Noordermeer and Duboule, 2013.

claim: Cells that activate Hox genes in a time sequence resolve the bivalent chromatin state and show two opposing distributions of histone marks over the HoxD cluster.
source: Subsequently, cells that activate these genes in a time sequence resolve this bivalent chromatin state and show two opposing distributions of histone marks over the HoxD cluster: transcribed genes carry large domains of H3K4me3 marks, whereas inactive genes are covered by H3K27me3 marks only (Soshnikova and Duboule, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Soshnikova and Duboule, 2009.

claim: Transcribed Hox genes carry large domains of H3K4me3 marks, whereas inactive genes are covered by H3K27me3 marks only.
source: Subsequently, cells that activate these genes in a time sequence resolve this bivalent chromatin state and show two opposing distributions of histone marks over the HoxD cluster: transcribed genes carry large domains of H3K4me3 marks, whereas inactive genes are covered by H3K27me3 marks only (Soshnikova and Duboule, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Soshnikova and Duboule, 2009.

claim: The same dichotomy in chromatin marks over Hox gene clusters was observed in various parts of the E10.5 embryonic trunk, in parallel with the spatial colinear distribution of transcripts.
source: The same dichotomy in chromatin marks over Hox gene clusters was observed in various parts of the E10.5 embryonic trunk, in parallel with the spatial colinear distribution of transcripts (Noordermeer et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Noordermeer et al., 2011.

claim: At E10.5, the 3D chromatin organization revealed a bi-modal compartmentalization, whereby active genes labeled by H3K4me3 are clustered together and physically separated from inactive genes labeled by H3K27me3.
source: The analysis of the 3D chromatin organization at this stage revealed a bi-modal compartmentalization, whereby active genes labeled by H3K4me3 are clustered together and physically separated from the inactive genes, labeled by H3K27me3 that are also found in a defined spatial structure (Noordermeer et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Noordermeer et al., 2011.

claim: The sizes of 3D compartments at Hox clusters correlate with the number of active vs inactive genes.
source: These 3D compartments, whose sizes correlate with the number of active vs inactive genes, may reinforce the proper maintenance of long-term transcriptional states at various AP levels by isolating Hox clusters from their surrounding chromatin and reducing interference between the active and inactive chromatin domains.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Noordermeer et al., 2011 and is an observation from that study.

claim: 3D compartments may reinforce the proper maintenance of long-term transcriptional states at various AP levels by isolating Hox clusters from their surrounding chromatin and reducing interference between active and inactive chromatin domains.
source: These 3D compartments, whose sizes correlate with the number of active vs inactive genes, may reinforce the proper maintenance of long-term transcriptional states at various AP levels by isolating Hox clusters from their surrounding chromatin and reducing interference between the active and inactive chromatin domains.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed based on the observed 3D organization.

claim: Distinct bimodal 3D organizations associated with transcriptional regulation at Hox clusters have been observed in other instances, either in the embryo or in mouse and human cultured cells.
source: Such distinct bimodal 3D organizations, associated with transcriptional regulation at Hox clusters, have been observed in other instances, either in the embryo (Montavon et al., 2011; Andrey et al., 2013) or in mouse and human cultured cells (Fraser et al., 2009; Ferraiuolo et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2011; Rousseau et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to Montavon et al., 2011; Andrey et al., 2013; Fraser et al., 2009; Ferraiuolo et al., 2010; Wang et al., 2011; Rousseau et al., 2014.

claim: In-embryo conformation studies were reported so far only in the context of spatial colinearity.
source: However, in-embryo conformation studies were reported so far only in the context of spatial colinearity, that is by comparing samples from different body levels at the same developmental stage.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of the field prior to this study.

claim: The stepwise activation of Hox genes occurs in parallel with their physical transition from a negative to a positive domain.
source: In this study, we describe the 3D organization of Hox gene clusters at high resolution during the implementation of temporal colinearity in the PSM and show that their stepwise activation occurs in parallel with their physical transition from a negative to a positive domain.
evidence: This is a main finding of the study, supported by 4C-seq data in Figures 2-4.

claim: The stepwise transition of genes from one domain to the other is accompanied by series of long-range contacts with the flanking gene deserts.
source: We also show that this process is accompanied by series of long-range contacts with the flanking gene deserts, even though these contacts remain largely invariable throughout temporal colinearity, unlike what was observed during limb development (Andrey et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a finding of the study, supported by data in Figure 5 and comparison to Andrey et al., 2013.

claim: Long-range contacts with flanking gene deserts remain largely invariable throughout temporal colinearity, unlike what was observed during limb development.
source: We also show that this process is accompanied by series of long-range contacts with the flanking gene deserts, even though these contacts remain largely invariable throughout temporal colinearity, unlike what was observed during limb development (Andrey et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a finding of the study, supported by data in Figure 5 and comparison to Andrey et al., 2013.

claim: Prior to their sequential activation, Hox genes are organized into local 3D chromatin compartments that encompass all bivalently marked chromatin.
source: Prior to their sequential activation, Hox genes are organized into local 3D chromatin compartments that encompass all bivalently marked chromatin (Bernstein et al., 2006).
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by 4C-seq data in Figure 1 and citation to Bernstein et al., 2006.

claim: In ES cells, 3D compartments at Hox clusters appear less defined than the fully inactive and H3K27me3-only marked compartments observed in differentiated cells.
source: In ES cells, however, these 3D compartments appear less defined than the fully inactive and H3K27me3-only marked compartments observed in differentiated cells.
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by comparison of 4C-seq data between ES cells and forebrain cells in Figure 1.

claim: The difference in discreteness of 3D compartments between ES cells and brain cells was paralleled by the amount of observable background transcription, which was substantially higher in ES cells.
source: This difference in discreteness was paralleled by the amount of observable background transcription, which was substantially higher in ES cells that in brain cells, though the biological impact of these very low level transcripts, if any, remains to be determined.
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by RNA-seq and RT-qPCR data in Figure 1—figure supplement 7.

claim: A generally relaxed chromatin organization in ES cells may accompany the plasticity required for cell-faith commitment.
source: This supports the view whereby a generally relaxed chromatin organization in ES cell may accompany the plasticity required for cell-faith commitment (Mattout and Meshorer, 2010).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citation to Mattout and Meshorer, 2010.

claim: In ES cells grown in the presence of two kinase-inhibitors, H3K27me3 marks are almost absent from Hox clusters.
source: Interestingly, in ES cells grown in the presence of two kinase-inhibitors and thought to be in a somehow more naïve developmental state, H3K27me3 marks are almost absent from Hox clusters (Marks et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Marks et al., 2012.

claim: Considering the high correlation between the presence of H3K27me3 marks and the existence of 3D chromatin compartments, Hox clusters within ES cells grown with kinase inhibitors would not be expected to group into 3D compartments as distinct as those visible in 'canonical' ES cells.
source: Considering the high correlation between the presence of H3K27me3 marks and the existence of 3D chromatin compartments, we would anticipate Hox clusters within these ES cells not to group into 3D compartments as distinct as those visible in 'canonical' ES cells.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the correlation observed in the study between H3K27me3 marks and 3D compartments.

claim: Structuring into fully inactive 3D compartments is a gradual process occurring over the course of several days during embryonic development.
source: We therefore hypothesize that structuring into fully inactive 3D compartments is a gradual process occurring over the course of several days during embryonic development.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their observations.

claim: The sequential transcriptional activation of Hox genes in the PSM coincides with a gene-by-gene transfer or positioning from the inactive H3K27me3-decorated compartment to a newly formed 3D compartment containing active genes only.
source: We also observe that the sequential transcriptional activation of Hox genes in the PSM coincides with a gene-by-gene transfer or positioning from the inactive H3K27me3-decorated compartment to a newly formed 3D compartment containing active genes only.
evidence: This is a main finding of the study supported by 4C-seq data in Figures 2-4.

claim: The presence of Hox genes in 3D compartments of various extents along the developed body axis is not an a posteriori mechanism used to fix and secure the long-term maintenance of various states of activity.
source: This indicates that the presence of Hox genes in 3D compartments of various extents, along the developed body axis (Noordermeer et al., 2011) is not an a posteriori mechanism used to fix and secure the long-term maintenance of various states of activity, fixed earlier by 'classical' transcriptional regulations acting in trans.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings, contrasting with a previous hypothesis.

claim: Spatial structures at Hox clusters are instrumental in the precise regulation of their transcriptional timing.
source: Instead, it suggests that such spatial structures are instrumental in the precise regulation of their transcriptional timing.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the data showing dynamic 3D reorganization during temporal colinearity.

claim: Temporal colinearity was originally proposed as a mechanism to translate time into spatial coordinates, in different ontogenic contexts.
source: Temporal colinearity was originally proposed as a mechanism to translate time into spatial coordinates, in different ontogenic contexts (Duboule, 1994; Gerard et al., 1997; Durston et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Duboule, 1994; Gerard et al., 1997; Durston et al., 2012.

claim: The transcriptional timing associated with gene clustering may not be an absolute prerequisite to achieve the proper spatial distributions of Hox genes products.
source: While our results support this idea, the transcriptional timing associated with gene clustering may not be an absolute prerequisite to achieve the proper spatial distributions of Hox genes products, as suggested by the multiple cases where single mammalian Hox transgenes could largely recapitulate the major expression specificities along the AP-axis (Krumlauf, 1994; Duboule, 2007; Tschopp et al., 2009; Tschopp and Duboule, 2011a).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Krumlauf, 1994; Duboule, 2007; Tschopp et al., 2009; Tschopp and Duboule, 2011a.

claim: The progressive transition of Hox genes from an inactive to an active 3D compartment may reflect a mechanism whose major aim is to protect the most 'posterior' Hox genes from premature exposure to activating factors.
source: In this context, it is possible that the progressive transition of Hox genes from an inactive to an active 3D compartment reflects the existence of a mechanism whose major aim would not be to precisely regulate a time sequence but instead, to protect the most 'posterior' Hox genes from a premature exposure to activating factors, a situation shown to block posterior elongation and hence to be detrimental to the embryo (Young et al., 2009; Mallo et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors, supported by citations to Young et al., 2009 and Mallo et al., 2010.

claim: Premature activation of posterior Hox genes blocks posterior elongation and is detrimental to the embryo.
source: In this context, it is possible that the progressive transition of Hox genes from an inactive to an active 3D compartment reflects the existence of a mechanism whose major aim would not be to precisely regulate a time sequence but instead, to protect the most 'posterior' Hox genes from a premature exposure to activating factors, a situation shown to block posterior elongation and hence to be detrimental to the embryo (Young et al., 2009; Mallo et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Young et al., 2009 and Mallo et al., 2010.

claim: The necessity to actively prevent the most posterior genes from premature activation is supported by their basal transcriptional activity in ES cells.
source: The necessity to actively prevent the most posterior genes from premature activation is supported by their basal transcriptional activity in ES cells, where Hox clusters are less discrete than in subsequent negative tissues such as fetal brain cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the RNA-seq data showing low-level transcription in ES cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 7).

claim: Studies using internal Hox cluster deletions and duplications showed that the relative position of Hox genes, rather than their promoters, determines their responses to activating signals.
source: Studies using internal Hox cluster deletions and duplications indeed showed that the relative position of Hox genes, rather than their promoters, determines their responses to activating signals (Tschopp et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tschopp et al., 2009.

claim: Graded signals emanating from the posterior aspect of the developing embryo would lead to a progressive de-repression of Hox clusters.
source: In this view, graded signals emanating from the posterior aspect of the developing embryo would lead to a progressive de-repression of Hox clusters, implying that these clusters would display some directional sensitivity.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: A link between activating factors and the segmentation clock was proposed.
source: While the nature of the activating factors is elusive, a link with the segmentation clock was proposed (Dubrulle et al., 2001; Zakany et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dubrulle et al., 2001 and Zakany et al., 2001.

claim: Polycomb group (Pc-G) gene products may play an important role in directional sensitivity of Hox clusters.
source: Concerning the directional sensitivity, Polycomb group (Pc-G) gene products may play an important role in this process, as the distribution of H3K27me3 marks correlate with the size of the inactive 3D compartments.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the correlation between H3K27me3 marks and 3D compartments observed in the study.

claim: A somewhat graded distribution of both EZH2 and RING1B was described over the HoxD cluster in ES cells, with the highest signals covering the most 'posterior' genes.
source: Recently, a somewhat graded distribution of both EZH2 and RING1B, two proteins members of the PRC2 and PRC1 complexes, respectively, was described over the HoxD cluster in ES cells, with the highest signals covering the most 'posterior' genes (Li et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Li et al., 2011.

claim: Directionality may derive from a weaker 'anterior' repression exerted by the Pc system.
source: Directionality may therefore derive from a weaker 'anterior' repression exerted by the Pc system.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on the graded distribution of Polycomb proteins.

claim: In Cbx2−/− mutant embryos, RA treatment resulted in premature yet colinear activation of Hoxd genes.
source: In this context, progressive alterations of the repressive system should sensitize the transcriptional threshold, while keeping on with directionality. This effect was observed in Cbx2−/− mutant embryos (a component of the PRC1 complex formerly known as M33), where the efficiency of the PRC1 complex was moderately decreased: RA treatment resulted in premature yet colinear activation of Hoxd genes (Bel-Vialar et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Bel-Vialar et al., 2000.

claim: Hox genes are originally activated in the most posterior aspect of the gastrulating embryo.
source: Hox genes are originally activated in the most posterior aspect of the gastrulating embryo.
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field.

claim: Initial activation of Hox genes seems to involve first a poised transcriptional status, followed by an apparent anterior forward spreading.
source: This initial wave of activation seems to involve first a poised transcriptional status (Forlani et al., 2003), followed by an apparent anterior forward spreading (Deschamps and Wijgerde, 1993; Gaunt and Strachan, 1994; Gaunt, 2001), which will ultimately lead to the positioning and initiation of the expression domains in the pre-somitic mesoderm (PSM).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Forlani et al., 2003; Deschamps and Wijgerde, 1993; Gaunt and Strachan, 1994; Gaunt, 2001.

claim: The colinear processing of the early phase of Hox activation may involve preparatory modifications in the chromatin status, making the system poised for activation by factors emanating from posterior cells.
source: The colinear processing of this early phase may involve preparatory modifications in the chromatin status, making the system poised for activation by factors emanating from posterior cells (Forlani et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Forlani et al., 2003.

claim: The observed anterior forward spreading in expressing cells may reflect a prolonged exposure to low levels of signals diffusing from the posterior end of the primitive streak.
source: In this view, the observed anterior forward spreading in expressing cells (Deschamps and Wijgerde, 1993; Gaunt and Strachan, 1994; Gaunt, 2001) may reflect a prolonged exposure to low levels of signals diffusing from the posterior end of the primitive streak (Forlani et al., 2003).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to Deschamps and Wijgerde, 1993; Gaunt and Strachan, 1994; Gaunt, 2001; Forlani et al., 2003.

claim: Once expression is established within the PSM, the boundary between the active and inactive compartments remains rather stable for the next couple of days, until the axial skeleton is fully determined.
source: However, our results suggest that once the expression is finally established within the PSM, the boundary between the active and inactive compartments remain rather stable for the next couple of days, until the axial skeleton is fully determined.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the comparison of samples at different developmental stages (Figures 3-4).

claim: Chromatin domains may represent part of the machinery used to fix a given state of activation and translate a temporal parameter into spatial coordinates.
source: In this view, these chromatin domains may represent part of the machinery used to fix a given state of activation and thus translate a temporal parameter into spatial coordinates.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their findings.

claim: Early heterochronies in Hox gene activation within the PSM will lead to subsequent re-positioning of the expression boundary.
source: As such, early heterochronies in Hox gene activation within the PSM will lead to subsequent re-positioning of the expression boundary, as previously observed (Gerard et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Gerard et al., 1997.

claim: The time-sequenced activation of Hoxd genes primarily uses regulatory influences located within the gene cluster itself.
source: By using genetic approaches, it was previously argued that the time-sequenced activation of Hoxd genes primarily uses regulatory influences located within the gene cluster itself (Spitz et al., 2001), with some contributions coming from more distant flanking regions (Tschopp et al., 2009; Tschopp and Duboule, 2011b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Spitz et al., 2001; Tschopp et al., 2009; Tschopp and Duboule, 2011b.

claim: Transcriptional activation of Hox genes is implemented with little-if any-differences in the interaction profiles between the target genes and their neighboring gene deserts, unlike the situation observed during limb development.
source: We now report that such a transcriptional activation is implemented with little-if any-differences in the interaction profiles between the target genes and their neighboring gene deserts, unlike the situation observed during limb development where new contacts appear upon gene activation (Montavon et al., 2011; Andrey et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a finding of the study supported by data in Figure 5 and comparison to Montavon et al., 2011 and Andrey et al., 2013.

claim: Temporal colinearity occurs within a framework of constitutive long-range interactions, which may provide a scaffold helping the bimodal separation of active and inactive genes to take place.
source: However, temporal colinearity does occur within a framework of constitutive long-range interactions, which may provide a scaffold helping the bimodal separation of active and inactive genes to take place.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the finding that long-range interactions remain largely stable (Figure 5).

claim: HiC analysis in ES cells identified a boundary between topological domains positioned around the Hoxd12 to Hoxd11 gene.
source: HiC analysis in ES cells identified a boundary between topological domains positioned around the Hoxd12 to Hoxd11 gene (Dixon et al., 2012; Figure 5—figure supplement 2D) and such boundaries are thought to impose or reflect a physical separation between the two interaction landscapes (e.g., Nora et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Dixon et al., 2012 and Nora et al., 2013.

claim: By using several viewpoints in a 4C set-up, the HoxD cluster in ES cells appears to form a single negative compartment, despite the interspersed presence of a TAD boundary.
source: Yet, by using several viewpoints in a 4C set-up, the HoxD cluster in ES cells appears to form a single negative compartment, despite the interspersed presence of this TAD boundary (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a finding of the study based on 4C-seq data in Figure 1.

claim: A detailed analysis of the HiC dataset reveals that the HoxD cluster itself forms a 'micro-TAD', displaying strong internal interactions.
source: In fact, a detailed analysis of the HiC dataset reveals that the HoxD cluster itself forms a 'micro-TAD', displaying strong internal interactions, in agreement with the 4C results reported here.
evidence: This is an analysis of published HiC data (Dixon et al., 2012) that reconciles it with the 4C-seq findings.

claim: The TAD boundary identified by HiC in ES cells represents an average description of two distinct configurations.
source: As such, we consider it likely that the TAD boundary identified by HiC in ES cells (Dixon et al., 2012) represents an average description of two distinct configurations (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors to reconcile HiC and 4C-seq data.

claim: For each allele, either the most posterior Hoxd13 gene forms stable interactions within the TAD on the centromeric side or, alternatively, the Hoxd11 to Hoxd1 genes interact with the TAD on the telomeric side.
source: For each allele, either the most posterior Hoxd13 gene forms stable interactions within the TAD on the centromeric side or, alternatively, the Hoxd11 to Hoxd1 genes interact with the TAD on the telomeric side (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors to explain the apparent paradox between HiC and 4C-seq data.

claim: For each allele, the entire HoxD 3D compartment becomes located towards a single TAD, on one side of the cluster with a physical separation from the other side.
source: As a consequence, for each allele the entire HoxD 3D compartment becomes located towards a single TAD, on one side of the cluster with a physical separation from the other side.
evidence: This is part of the hypothesis proposed to reconcile HiC and 4C-seq data.

claim: The CTCF protein binds multiple sites around the Hoxd13 to Hoxd8 region.
source: The CTCF protein, which may play a role in scaffolding TADs, binds multiple sites around the Hoxd13 to Hoxd8 region (Ferraiuolo et al., 2010; Phillips-Cremins et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ferraiuolo et al., 2010 and Phillips-Cremins et al., 2013.

claim: At later stages, when the HoxD cluster adopts a bimodal 3D organization, the tethering of interactions may help implement the separation between activated and repressed Hox genes.
source: At later stages, when the HoxD cluster adopts a bimodal 3D organization, the tethering of interactions, as illustrated by the existence of TADs on either side, may help implement the separation between activated and repressed Hox genes, thereby potentially reducing deleterious regulatory interferences and premature activation of the most posterior Hox genes.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors about the functional role of TADs.

claim: Embryonic 4C-seq samples consisted of pooled material from 129 embryos for E8.5 pre-somatic mesoderm samples.
source: Embryonic 4C-seq samples consisted of pooled material from multiple embryos: 129 embryos for E8.5 pre-somatic mesoderm samples, 196 embryos for E9.5 tail bud, 143 embryos for E10.5 tail bud or E10.5 lumbo-sacral trunks and around 20 embryos for each E10.5 forebrain sample.
evidence: This is a methodological detail from the Materials and methods section.

claim: Embryonic 4C-seq samples consisted of pooled material from 196 embryos for E9.5 tail bud.
source: Embryonic 4C-seq samples consisted of pooled material from multiple embryos: 129 embryos for E8.5 pre-somatic mesoderm samples, 196 embryos for E9.5 tail bud, 143 embryos for E10.5 tail bud or E10.5 lumbo-sacral trunks and around 20 embryos for each E10.5 forebrain sample.
evidence: This is a methodological detail from the Materials and methods section.

claim: Embryonic 4C-seq samples consisted of pooled material from 143 embryos for E10.5 tail bud or E10.5 lumbo-sacral trunks.
source: Embryonic 4C-seq samples consisted of pooled material from multiple embryos: 129 embryos for E8.5 pre-somatic mesoderm samples, 196 embryos for E9.5 tail bud, 143 embryos for E10.5 tail bud or E10.5 lumbo-sacral trunks and around 20 embryos for each E10.5 forebrain sample.
evidence: This is a methodological detail from the Materials and methods section.

claim: Embryonic 4C-seq samples consisted of pooled material from around 20 embryos for each E10.5 forebrain sample.
source: Embryonic 4C-seq samples consisted of pooled material from multiple embryos: 129 embryos for E8.5 pre-somatic mesoderm samples, 196 embryos for E9.5 tail bud, 143 embryos for E10.5 tail bud or E10.5 lumbo-sacral trunks and around 20 embryos for each E10.5 forebrain sample.
evidence: This is a methodological detail from the Materials and methods section.

claim: In ES cells, the overall size of the strong interaction profiles exactly matched the distribution of bivalent chromatin marks.
source: The overall size of the strong interaction profiles exactly matched the distribution of bivalent chromatin marks in these cells, with a moderate level of H3K27me3 covering the cluster and rather weak H3K4me3 peaks labeling promoters (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplements 1–4; Bernstein et al., 2006; Soshnikova and Duboule, 2009).
evidence: This is a finding supported by comparison of 4C-seq and ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 1A and supplementary figures.

claim: In ES cells, Hox clusters display a moderate level of H3K27me3 covering the cluster and rather weak H3K4me3 peaks labeling promoters.
source: The overall size of the strong interaction profiles exactly matched the distribution of bivalent chromatin marks in these cells, with a moderate level of H3K27me3 covering the cluster and rather weak H3K4me3 peaks labeling promoters (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplements 1–4; Bernstein et al., 2006; Soshnikova and Duboule, 2009).
evidence: This is shown in Figure 1A and supplementary figures, and supported by citations to Bernstein et al., 2006 and Soshnikova and Duboule, 2009.

claim: In ES cells, Hox genes interacted more with the outside chromatin, relative to their interactions within the cluster, as compared to forebrain cells.
source: A more quantitative comparison in 3D architectures between ES cells and E10.5 forebrain cells nevertheless indicated that in ES cells, Hox genes interacted more with the outside chromatin, relative to their interactions within the cluster, as compared to forebrain cells (Figure 1B,C, Figure 1—figure supplements 1–5).
evidence: This is a finding supported by quantitative analysis shown in Figure 1B,C and supplementary figures.

claim: In embryonic forebrain cells, HoxB forms a single 3D compartment, excluding the 80 kb large repeat-rich intergenic region located between Hoxb13 and Hoxb9, which loops out.
source: In embryonic forebrain cells, HoxB forms a single 3D compartment, excluding the 80 kb large repeat-rich intergenic region located between Hoxb13 and Hoxb9, which loops out (Noordermeer et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Noordermeer et al., 2011.

claim: In ES cells, both the Hoxb13 and Hoxb9 viewpoints revealed local 3D compartments matching the extent of bivalent histone marks, yet these two compartments remained separated and did not fuse.
source: In contrast, both the Hoxb13 and Hoxb9 viewpoints revealed local 3D compartments in ES cells, matching again the extent of bivalent histone marks, yet these two compartments remained separated and did not fuse.
evidence: This is a finding supported by 4C-seq data shown in Figure 1B and supplementary figures.

claim: In ES cells, the HoxB cluster is organized in two 3D compartments, which have more interactions with their genomic surroundings than in forebrain cells.
source: In ES cells, the HoxB cluster is thus organized in two 3D compartments, which have more interactions with their genomic surroundings than in forebrain cells (Figure 1D, right and Figure 1—figure supplement 6B).
evidence: This is a finding supported by 4C-seq data shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 6B.

claim: In both ES and brain cells, H3K27me3 marks strongly correlated with the 3D organization.
source: In both cell types, H3K27me3 marks strongly correlated with the 3D organization, suggesting a direct link between these two readouts.
evidence: This is a finding based on correlation analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: No particular correlation was observed between the 3D organization and the presence of H3K4me3 marks in the bivalent state.
source: In contrast, no particular correlation was observed between the 3D organization and the presence of H3K4me3 marks, in the bivalent state (Table 1), suggesting that H3K4me3 marks and/or the associated factors do not noticeably contribute to the formation of 3D compartments in ES cells.
evidence: This is a finding based on correlation analysis shown in Table 1.

claim: H3K4me3 marks and/or the associated factors do not noticeably contribute to the formation of 3D compartments in ES cells.
source: In contrast, no particular correlation was observed between the 3D organization and the presence of H3K4me3 marks, in the bivalent state (Table 1), suggesting that H3K4me3 marks and/or the associated factors do not noticeably contribute to the formation of 3D compartments in ES cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the lack of correlation shown in Table 1.

claim: In ES cells, RNA-seq detected transcription for most Hox genes, though generally at very low level.
source: In ES cells, RNA-seq detected transcription for most Hox genes, though generally at very low level (Figure 1—figure supplement 7A,B).
evidence: This is a finding supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7A,B.

claim: RT-qPCR confirmed that some low-level transcripts in ES cells (particularly the Hoxd13 and Hoxb13 transcripts) constitute genuine processed transcripts.
source: RT-qPCR of a subset of transcripts confirmed that some of these low-level transcripts (particularly the Hoxd13 and Hoxb13 transcripts) constitute genuine processed transcripts (Figure 1—figure supplement 7C).
evidence: This is a finding supported by RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7C.

claim: In E10.5 forebrain cells, transcription of Hox genes was rarely detected, and no reliable spliced transcripts were detected.
source: In contrast, transcription of Hox genes in E10.5 forebrain cells was rarely detected, and no reliable spliced transcripts were detected (Figure 1—figure supplement 7).
evidence: This is a finding supported by RNA-seq and RT-qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 7.

claim: When Hox genes are decorated by bivalent chromatin marks, they appear more permissive for background transcription as compared to other cell types where they are covered by H3K27me3 marks only.
source: Therefore, when Hox genes are decorated by bivalent chromatin marks, they appear more permissive for background transcription as compared to other cell types where they are covered by H3K27me3 marks only, likely illustrating the increased resistance to transcription of the latter condition.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on the comparison of transcription levels between ES cells and forebrain cells.

claim: In ES cells, posterior Hox genes seem to be more prone to background transcriptional activation than more anterior Hox genes.
source: In this context, posterior Hox genes seems to be more prone to background transcriptional activation in ES cells than more anterior Hox genes, in contrast to their subsequent dynamics of activation in future embryonic tissues where anterior genes come first.
evidence: This is an observation based on RNA-seq data in Figure 1—figure supplement 7A.

claim: The higher background transcription of posterior Hox genes in ES cells may reflect the presence of strong enhancers in their vicinity.
source: This may reflect the presence of strong enhancers in their vicinity (Montavon et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citation to Montavon et al., 2011.

claim: E8.5 PSM samples were dissected at Theiler stage 13, posterior from the approximate level of the 12th to 14th forming somite.
source: For this purpose, we compared the 4C-seq profiles from ES cells with those obtained from early embryonic E8.5 PSM cells dissected out at Theiler stage 13, posterior from the approximate level of the 12th to 14th forming somite (Figure 2A, scheme; Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the sample preparation.

claim: In the E8.5 PSM sample, transcriptional activation had progressed up to the Hoxd9 gene, whereas the Hoxd10 to Hoxd13 loci remained silent.
source: In the most caudal aspect of this latter cellular territory, transcriptional activation had progressed up to the Hoxd9 gene, whereas the Hoxd10 to Hoxd13 loci remained silent (Soshnikova and Duboule, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Soshnikova and Duboule, 2009.

claim: The E8.5 PSM cellular population was composed of a mixture of cells positive and negative for Hoxd9 expression, whereas all cells were negative for Hoxd13.
source: This cellular population was thus composed of a mixture of cells positive and negative for Hoxd9 expression, whereas all cells were negative for Hoxd13.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known expression patterns and the dissection level.

claim: In the E8.5 PSM sample, the majority of cells expressed Hoxd4.
source: Conversely, the majority of cells expressed Hoxd4.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known expression patterns and the dissection level.

claim: In E8.5 PSM, the inactive Hoxd13 viewpoint interacted mostly with the domain labeled by H3K27me3, at the centromeric side of the cluster.
source: The inactive Hoxd13 viewpoint interacted mostly with the domain labeled by H3K27me3, at the centromeric side of the cluster (Figure 2A, bottom left).
evidence: This is a finding supported by 4C-seq data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: In E8.5 PSM, the active Hoxd4 gene essentially interacted with the other transcribed genes on the telomeric side of the cluster, labeled by H3K4me3 marks.
source: In contrast, the active Hoxd4 gene essentially interacted with the other transcribed genes on the telomeric side of the cluster, labeled by H3K4me3 marks (Figure 2A, bottom right).
evidence: This is a finding supported by 4C-seq data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The same bi-modal 3D organization was observed for all Hox gene clusters in E8.5 PSM.
source: The same bi-modal 3D organization was observed for all Hox gene clusters (Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is a finding supported by 4C-seq data shown in Figure 2—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: At both E8.5 and E10.5 stages where Hox clusters are partially active, the patterns of 3D compartmentalization and histone marks strongly correlated.
source: At both stages where Hox clusters are partially active, the patterns of 3D compartmentalization and histone marks thus strongly correlated.
evidence: This is a finding based on correlation analysis shown in Figure 2B and Table 1.

claim: Step wise Hox gene transcriptional activation is accompanied by a conformational separation between active and inactive domains, which pre-figures their 3D organization at later developmental stages along the AP-axis.
source: Therefore, step wise Hox gene transcriptional activation, at least for the Hoxd9 to Hoxd13 genes, is accompanied by a conformational separation between active and inactive domains, which pre-figures their 3D organization at later developmental stages along the AP-axis (Figure 2; Noordermeer et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the data shown in Figure 2 and comparison to Noordermeer et al., 2011.

claim: Studies on the global transcriptional organization of the HoxD cluster in the developing spinal cord revealed two large and regulatory-independent modules, which separate 'posterior' genes (the AbdB-related Hoxd9 to Hoxd13 genes) from the rest of the gene cluster.
source: However, studies on the global transcriptional organization of the HoxD cluster, at least in the developing spinal cord, revealed two large and regulatory-independent modules, which separate 'posterior' genes (the AbdB-related Hoxd9 to Hoxd13 genes) from the rest of the gene cluster (Tschopp et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tschopp et al., 2012.

claim: In different developmental contexts such as the limbs and the cecum, groups of neighboring Hoxd genes are activated as single regulatory blocks.
source: Also, in different developmental contexts such as the limbs and the cecum, groups of neighboring Hoxd genes are activated as single regulatory blocks (Montavon et al., 2011; Andrey et al., 2013; Delpretti et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Montavon et al., 2011; Andrey et al., 2013; Delpretti et al., 2013.

claim: The E9.5 tail bud sample was obtained after cutting off the most caudal part of E9.5 embryos (Theiler stage 15) right after the incipient hind limb bud, at ca. somite 26–27 level.
source: This latter sample was obtained after cutting off the most caudal part of E9.5 embryos (Theiler stage 15) right after the incipient hind limb bud, that is at ca. somite 26–27 level.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the sample preparation.

claim: The E9.5 tail bud sample contained the tail bud proper as well as some tissue localized slightly more rostral.
source: Accordingly, this sample contained the tail bud proper as well as some tissue localized slightly more rostral.
evidence: This is a description of the sample composition.

claim: During the 24 hr time interval between E8.5 and E9.5, the Hoxd10 and Hoxd11 genes become robustly activated.
source: During this 24 hr time interval, the Hoxd10 and Hoxd11 genes become robustly activated in these cells, which are derived from a sub-population of the sample dissected at E8.5.
evidence: This is an inference based on known developmental timing and expression patterns.

claim: In the E8.5 PSM, Hoxd10 and Hoxd11 are still silenced.
source: In the E8.5 PSM, Hoxd10 and Hoxd11 are still silenced.
evidence: This is based on known expression patterns at this developmental stage.

claim: When switching from an inactive to an active state, Hoxd11 re-deployed its interactions from the inactive, centromeric compartment to the active telomeric compartment.
source: When switching from an inactive to an active state, Hoxd11 re-deployed its interactions from the inactive, centromeric compartment (Figure 3, top ratio: blue shaded area) to the active telomeric compartment (Figure 3, top ratio: brown shaded area).
evidence: This is a finding supported by 4C-seq data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Hoxd4 shifted its interactions towards the centromeric (active) part of the cluster in both E9.5 and E10.5 samples.
source: Accordingly, Hoxd4 shifted its interactions towards the centromeric (active) part of the cluster in both E9.5 and E10.5 samples (Figure 3; right), to contact Hoxd10, Hoxd11 and, to some extent, Hoxd12 (Figure 3, top ratio: brown shaded area).
evidence: This is a finding supported by 4C-seq data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The dissected E8.5 PSM contained a mixture of cells either positive or negative for Hoxd9 transcription, which coincided with this gene showing conspicuous contacts with both extremities of the gene cluster.
source: Of note, the dissected E8.5 PSM contained a mixture of cells either positive or negative for Hoxd9 transcription, which coincided with this gene showing conspicuous contacts with both extremities of the gene cluster, depending whether it was active (right) or inactive (left) (Figure 3, top, black arrows).
evidence: This is a finding supported by 4C-seq data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The E9.5 dissection contains a more homogenous cell population, strongly expressing Hoxd9.
source: In contrast, the E9.5 dissection contains a more homogenous cell population, strongly expressing this gene.
evidence: This is an inference based on the dissection level and known expression patterns.

claim: In the E9.5 sample, Hoxd9 contacts more strongly the now expressed Hoxd10 and Hoxd11 genes, whereas the interactions with Hoxd13 or Evx2 are strongly diminished.
source: As a consequence, in this latter sample, Hoxd9 contacts more strongly the now expressed Hoxd10 and Hoxd11 genes, whereas the interactions with Hoxd13 or Evx2 are strongly diminished (Figure 3; compare top with middle panels).
evidence: This is a finding supported by 4C-seq data shown in Figure 3.

claim: In the E10.5 tail bud, the terminal part of the cluster containing Hoxd12 and Hoxd13 has been activated.
source: In the E10.5 tail bud, the terminal part of the cluster containing Hoxd12 and Hoxd13 has been activated, as shown by the increased contacts established by Hoxd13 with the telomeric part of the cluster, indicating that the full HoxD array had been processed and that all genes were now (at least in part) included into a 'positive' compartment (Figure 3, bottom ratio: purple shading).
evidence: This is a finding supported by 4C-seq data shown in Figure 3.

claim: In the E10.5 tail bud, contacts of Hoxd13 with the telomeric part of the cluster were weak, most likely reflecting the restricted expression of Hoxd13 at this stage, in a small subset of the dissected cells.
source: While considerably increased, contacts of Hoxd13 with the telomeric part of the cluster were however weak (Figure 3, bottom, black arrows), most likely reflecting the restricted expression of Hoxd13 at this stage, in a small subset of the dissected cells.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the 4C-seq data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Contacts established both by Hoxd4 and Hoxd9 with the centromeric part of the cluster extended towards the end of the cluster along with the developmental stage.
source: In the same context, contacts established both by Hoxd4 and Hoxd9 with the centromeric part of the cluster extended towards the end of the cluster along with the developmental stage, such that both reached Hoxd12 in E10.5 samples, whereas Hoxd13 was only weakly contacted, corresponding to the results obtained when using Hoxd13 as a bait (Figure 3; bottom left).
evidence: This is a finding supported by 4C-seq data shown in Figure 3.

claim: The colinear time sequence in Hox genes activation is paralleled by a progressive transition in the chromatin structure, with a positive domain gaining in size along with time, at the expense of the negative domain.
source: Therefore, it appears that the colinear time sequence in Hox genes activation is paralleled by a progressive transition in the chromatin structure, with a positive domain gaining in size along with time, at the expense of the negative domain, as best seen by the extension of Hoxd4 contacts.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the temporal series of 4C-seq data shown in Figure 3.

claim: At E8.5, Hoxd4 interactions extended up to Hoxd8-Hoxd9.
source: At E8.5, these interactions extended up to Hoxd8-Hoxd9.
evidence: This is a finding from the 4C-seq data shown in Figure 3.

claim: In E9.5 samples, Hoxd10 was clearly contacted by Hoxd4.
source: In E9.5 samples Hoxd10 was clearly contacted, and in E10.5 Hoxd11 and Hoxd12 were also involved (Figure 3, right column).
evidence: This is a finding from the 4C-seq data shown in Figure 3.

claim: In E10.5 samples, Hoxd11 and Hoxd12 were contacted by Hoxd4.
source: In E9.5 samples Hoxd10 was clearly contacted, and in E10.5 Hoxd11 and Hoxd12 were also involved (Figure 3, right column).
evidence: This is a finding from the 4C-seq data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Dynamic topologies suggest a stepwise transition of the genes from the negative to the positive compartment, rather than the switch of large groups of multiple transcription units.
source: These dynamic topologies suggest a stepwise transition of the genes from the negative to the positive compartment, rather than the switch of large groups of multiple transcription units, following a discrete and global chromatin re-organization.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the progressive changes observed in the 4C-seq data.

claim: During axial extension, Hox genes are activated in the most posterior aspect of the elongating embryo.
source: During axial extension, Hox genes are activated in the most posterior aspect of the elongating embryo (Deschamps and van Nes, 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Deschamps and van Nes, 2005.

claim: Cells implementing the stepwise transition in chromatin domains can fix and memorize their bimodal distribution once they exit the posterior zone of activation.
source: It is thus possible that cells implementing this stepwise transition in chromatin domains can fix and memorize their bimodal distribution once they exit the posterior zone of activation, leading to the colinear Hox conformations observed along the AP-axis (Noordermeer et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors, supported by citation to Noordermeer et al., 2011.

claim: The profile obtained from E8.5 PSM globally aligned with that observed in the 'anterior trunk' sample at E10.5.
source: The profile obtained from E8.5 PSM (Figure 3, top), right at the onset of Hoxd9 activation globaly aligned with that observed in the 'anterior trunk' sample at E10.5 (Figure 4, top), that is a cellular domain with a posterior boundary positioned approximately at the Hoxd9 anterior limit of expression.
evidence: This is a finding based on comparison of 4C-seq profiles shown in Figures 3 and 4.

claim: At E9.5 (Theiler stage 14), the 'tail bud' was dissected from ca. somite 22 to 25 and caudally.
source: At E9.5 (Theiler stage 14), the 'tail bud' (i.e., from the start of the non-segmented mesoderm) was dissected from ca. somite 22 to 25 and caudally.
evidence: This is a methodological detail describing the sample preparation.

claim: At E9.5, Hoxd9 is robustly transcribed, whereas Hoxd11 has just started transcriptional activation.
source: At this stage, Hoxd9 is robustly transcribed, whereas Hoxd11 has just started transcriptional activation.
evidence: This is based on known expression patterns at this developmental stage.

claim: The interaction profiles obtained in E9.5 tail bud tissue were most similar to those obtained when a fragment of E10.5 trunk was dissected out that grossly corresponded to the future lumbo-sacral region, at levels 22 to 28.
source: The interaction profiles obtained in this tissue were most similar to those obtained when a fragment of E10.5 trunk was dissected out that grossly corresponded to the future lumbo-sacral region, at levels 22 to 28, that is the AP levels supposedly produced in the E9.5 tail bud (Figure 4, middle).
evidence: This is a finding based on comparison of 4C-seq profiles shown in Figure 4.

claim: In the E10.5 lumbo-sacral sample, neither Hoxd12 nor Hoxd13 are as yet transcribed.
source: In this lumbo-sacral sample, neither Hoxd12 nor Hoxd13 are as yet transcribed, which coincided with the absence of contact between Hoxd13 and the active part of the gene cluster (Figure 4, middle, left).
evidence: This is a finding based on 4C-seq data shown in Figure 4.

claim: In the E10.5 lumbo-sacral sample, Hoxd11 displayed a mixed interaction profile, contacting both the negative and positive domains, likely reflecting the presence of both expressing and non-expressing cells.
source: On the other hand, Hoxd11 expectedly displayed a mixed interaction profile, contacting both the negative and positive domains, likely reflecting the presence of both expressing and non-expressing cells (Figure 4, middle).
evidence: This is a finding and interpretation based on 4C-seq data shown in Figure 4.

claim: In the most caudal piece of the E10.5 mouse embryo, interactions between Hoxd12, Hoxd13 and the positive domain were detected, suggesting that the entire cluster falls into a single spatial domain.
source: In the most caudal piece of the E10.5 mouse embryo, interactions between Hoxd12, Hoxd13 and the positive domain were finally detected, suggesting that the entire cluster falls into a single spatial domain (Figure 4, bottom ratio: purple shading).
evidence: This is a finding and interpretation based on 4C-seq data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The bimodal distributions are frozen in cells leaving the zone of proliferation, at the caudal aspect of the embryo where temporal colinearity is potentially processed.
source: Based on these data, we propose that the bimodal distributions are frozen in those cells leaving the zone of proliferation, at the caudal aspect of the embryo where temporal colinearity is potentially processed.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on the comparison of temporal and spatial samples.

claim: 3D structures and Hox transcription programs are maintained and memorize the various AP levels from which they originate.
source: These 3D structures, and hence the Hox transcription programs, will thus be maintained and memorize the various AP levels from which they originate.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the comparison of temporal and spatial samples.

claim: In different developmental contexts, the transcriptional activity of Hoxd genes coincides with an overall remodeling of long-range chromatin interactions with the flanking gene deserts.
source: In different developmental contexts, the transcriptional activity of Hoxd genes coincides with an overall remodeling of long-range chromatin interactions with the flanking gene deserts, which harbor essential enhancer elements active in these developing tissues (Montavon et al., 2011; Andrey et al., 2013; Berlivet et al., 2013; Delpretti et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Montavon et al., 2011; Andrey et al., 2013; Berlivet et al., 2013; Delpretti et al., 2013.

claim: Colinear activation of Hoxd genes along the developing trunk is thought to primarily rely on regulatory influences intrinsic to the gene cluster itself.
source: Colinear activation of Hoxd genes along the developing trunk is thought to primarily rely on regulatory influences intrinsic to the gene cluster itself (Spitz et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Spitz et al., 2001.

claim: Contributions of the flanking regulatory landscapes in temporal colinearity have been proposed.
source: However, and even though their importance remains unclear, contributions of the flanking regulatory landscapes in this process have been proposed (Tschopp et al., 2009; Tschopp and Duboule, 2011b).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tschopp et al., 2009 and Tschopp and Duboule, 2011b.

claim: All interrogated Hoxd genes displayed substantial interactions with the flanking gene deserts.
source: By using a recently developed analytical methodology (Woltering et al., 2014), we found that all interrogated Hoxd genes displayed substantial interactions with the flanking gene deserts (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is a finding supported by 4C-seq data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Quantification of interactions over both the centromeric and telomeric gene deserts revealed a gene-specific interaction preference towards either one or the other desert.
source: The quantification of interactions over both the centromeric and telomeric gene deserts revealed a gene-specific interaction preference towards either one or the other desert (Figure 5B), similar to what was previously described in limb bud cells (Montavon et al., 2011; Andrey et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 5B and comparison to Montavon et al., 2011 and Andrey et al., 2013.

claim: The dynamics of long-range chromatin interactions were moderate, if any, and no clear modification in the contact profiles were detected between the inactive state in ES cells and subsequent transcriptional activation.
source: However, in marked contrast, the dynamics of these long-range chromatin interactions were moderate, if any, and no clear modification in the contact profiles were detected between the inactive state in ES cells, and the subsequent transcriptional activation (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: This is a finding supported by data shown in Figure 5B,C.

claim: Hierarchical clustering of global patterns of long-range interactions revealed that the Hoxd4, Hoxd9 and Hoxd11 viewpoints systematically cluster together, whereas the Hoxd13 viewpoint always behaves as outlier.
source: Hierarchical clustering of global patterns of long-range interactions revealed that the Hoxd4, Hoxd9 and Hoxd11 viewpoints systematically cluster together, whereas the Hoxd13 viewpoint always behaves as outlier (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a finding supported by hierarchical clustering analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The clustering of interactions matches with the position of a previously mapped boundary between 'topological associated domains' (TADs).
source: This clustering of interactions matches with the position of a previously mapped boundary between 'topological associated domains' (TADs; Dixon et al., 2012; Nora et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an interpretation based on comparison to published TAD data from Dixon et al., 2012 and Nora et al., 2012.

claim: In ES cells, two TADs cover approximately the gene deserts on either side and have their border at the level of the Hoxd12-Hoxd11 genes.

claim: Virtual 4C from HiC data with bins that cover the Hoxd genes show highly similar priming of interactions with the surrounding TADs when compared to 4C-seq analysis.
source: Virtual 4C from HiC data with bins that cover the Hoxd genes show highly similar priming of interactions with the surrounding TADs when compared to our 4C-seq analysis, confirming that both approaches score similar chromatin behavior (Figure 5—figure supplement 2; Sexton et al., 2012 for analysis strategy).
evidence: This is a finding based on comparison of virtual 4C from HiC data and 4C-seq data, shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: During limb development, genes located near the TAD boundary (Hoxd9 to Hoxd11) change their tropism and switch their contacts from one TAD to the other.
source: During limb development, genes located near this boundary (Hoxd9 to Hoxd11) change their tropism and switch their contacts from one TAD to the other, such as to interact sequentially with the appropriate enhancers (Andrey et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Andrey et al., 2013.

claim: During temporal colinearity, structural re-organization of TAD interactions is not observed and the stepwise transcriptional activation of Hoxd genes appears to occur within a largely constitutive framework of long-range interactions.
source: During temporal colinearity, however, such structural re-organization is not observed and hence the stepwise transcriptional activation of Hoxd genes appears to occur within a largely constitutive framework of long-range interactions; genes up to Hoxd11 interact mostly with the telomeric domain, either before or after their activation, and Hoxd13 always interacts with the centromeric domain.
evidence: This is a finding based on the long-range interaction analysis shown in Figure 5 and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.
